slides.0.title: Red winemaking, maturation and bottling
slides.0.subtitle: How much to extract and how long to age: the two dials of red style
slides.1.title: Extraction
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Destemming and cold soak
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Most reds are destemmed first; a few days of pre-fermentation cold soak extracts colour and fruit in the absence of alcohol, with less tannin
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Punching down, pumping over and délestage
slides.1.highlights.1.content: During fermentation the skins form a cap: punching down extracts strongly yet gently, pumping over also aerates and cools, and délestage (rack-and-return) extracts more while giving softer tannins
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Temperature and maceration length
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Reds usually ferment at about 20–32°C, with warmer temperatures extracting more; extended post-fermentation maceration lets tannins polymerise and soften, though too long risks over-extraction
slides.1.content: The aim of extraction is ripe tannin, not the most tannin.
slides.2.title: Whole bunch, carbonic maceration and pressing
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Whole-bunch fermentation
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Keeping some or all stems adds spice, herbal notes and structure and freshens the fruit; but unripe stems bring green tannins
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Carbonic maceration
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Whole bunches in a sealed CO₂-filled vat ferment inside the berry, giving cherry, banana and bubblegum notes and soft, low-tannin wines; Beaujolais is the classic example, and Languedoc Carignan often uses it
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Free-run and press wine
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Free-run wine that drains after fermentation is finer; press wine is heavier in tannin and colour. The winemaker can add press wine according to the vintage to adjust structure
slides.2.content: Pair technique with style in essays: whole bunch → spice and freshness; carbonic → fruitiness and softness.
slides.3.title: Maturation, clarification and bottling
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Vessels and oxygen
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Small oak barrels add oak flavour and micro-oxygenation, most strongly when new; large casks, concrete and clay have less influence and emphasise fruit and place. French oak leans to spice and fine tannins, American oak to vanilla and coconut
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Fining and stabilisation
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Fining agents (e.g. egg white, bentonite) remove haze or harsh compounds; cold stabilisation prevents tartrate crystals; filtration removes microbes. Unfined, unfiltered wine is a style choice at the cost of stability risk
slides.3.highlights.2.title: SO₂ and closures
slides.3.highlights.2.content: SO₂ is antioxidant and antimicrobial. Natural cork admits tiny amounts of oxygen but can carry TCA cork taint; screwcaps seal consistently and keep fruit but can show reduction; synthetic closures sit in between
slides.3.content: Every step before bottling trades stability against character.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is the most typical style result of carbonic maceration?
C. High tannin, needing long ageing
D. Fruity, low in tannin, soft
What is the main purpose of a pre-fermentation cold soak?
D. Extract colour and fruit without alcohol present
Cold soak extracts relatively little tannin.
What does cold stabilisation mainly prevent?
Cold stabilisation drops potassium bitartrate out before bottling.
TCA taint is most associated with which closure?
The risk with screwcaps is reduction instead.
